competencies.text: Describe human modification of landforms since Neolithic (~6,000 BCE).
Assess hazards (tropical cyclones, ipo-ipo, thunderstorms, storm surges, heat waves).

days.title: Human Impact on Landforms
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

By the end of today's lesson, you will be able to describe how humans have modified landforms since the Neolithic period (~6,000 BCE), assess common hazards in the Philippines, and evaluate how human activities increase or reduce hazard risk.

🌾 Human Modification of Landforms Through Time

Humans have reshaped Earth's surface for thousands of years. This is called anthropogenic modification — changes caused by human activity.

EraTimeHuman ModificationImpact on Landforms
Neolithic~6,000 BCESlash-and-burn farming, early settlementsSmall clearings, terraced hillsides (e.g., early rice terraces)
Ancient civilizations3,000 BCE–500 CEIrrigation canals, dams, stone citiesRivers diverted; floodplains modified
Medieval500–1,500 CEDeforestation for farmland and timberSoil erosion; hillside clearing
Industrial era1700s–1900sMining, railways, urban expansionMountains carved; valleys filled; coastlines altered
Modern era1950s–presentMega-dams, highways, reclamation, mega-citiesMassive reshaping of rivers, coasts, and urban terrain

🏙️ Types of Human Modification

ActivityEffect on LandformsExample in the Philippines
DeforestationRemoves root systems → soil erosion, landslidesIllegal logging in Sierra Madre
MiningRemoves topsoil, creates open pits, tailings damsMarcopper disaster (Marinduque, 1996)
UrbanizationCovers land with concrete → less absorption, more floodingMetro Manila flood-prone areas
AgricultureTerraces, rice paddies, canals reshape slopesBanaue Rice Terraces, Central Luzon
ReclamationAdds land along coasts — changes wave patternsManila Bay reclamation projects
Dam constructionAlters river flow, traps sedimentSan Roque Dam (Pangasinan), Pantabangan Dam
Road buildingCuts into mountainsides — creates landslide riskCordillera and Sierra Madre highways

⚠️ Natural Hazards in the Philippines

A hazard is a natural event that can cause damage, injury, or loss of life. A disaster happens when a hazard strikes a vulnerable community.

🌀 Tropical Cyclones (Typhoons)

  • About 20 enter Philippine waters each year
  • Bring strong winds, heavy rain, storm surges, and flooding
  • Worst example: Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan, 2013) — 6,300+ deaths

🌪️ Ipo-Ipo (Tornadoes/Waterspouts)

  • Small, intense rotating columns of air
  • Common during thunderstorms and typhoon season
  • Can cause localized damage in minutes
  • Also called whirlwinds or buhawi in Filipino

⛈️ Thunderstorms

  • Produce lightning, thunder, heavy rain, and strong winds
  • Can trigger flash floods, hail, and ipo-ipo
  • Very common in the Philippines, especially in the afternoon during the rainy season

🌊 Storm Surges

  • Abnormal sea-level rise near the coast during a typhoon
  • Most destructive in low-lying coastal communities
  • Yolanda's storm surge reached 5–7 meters — the main cause of deaths

🔥 Heat Waves

  • Prolonged periods of abnormally high temperature
  • Combined with high humidity, the heat index can reach dangerous levels (41°C+)
  • Risks: heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke
  • Vulnerable: children, elderly, outdoor workers, athletes

📊 How Human Activities Increase or Reduce Hazard Risk

Human ActivityEffect on Hazard Risk
Deforestation⬆️ Increases landslide, flood, and erosion risk
Improper waste disposal⬆️ Increases flood risk (clogged drains)
Building on floodplains⬆️ Increases flood damage
Coastal reclamation without planning⬆️ Increases storm surge vulnerability
Reforestation & mangrove restoration⬇️ Reduces flood, landslide, and storm surge risk
Proper urban planning⬇️ Reduces flooding and structural damage
Early warning systems⬇️ Reduces casualties via evacuation
Community DRRM training⬇️ Reduces disaster impact on people

🇵🇭 Philippine Agencies Managing Hazards

  • PAGASA — typhoons, floods, heat index, rainfall warnings
  • PHIVOLCS — earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunami warnings
  • NDRRMC — national disaster response coordination
  • MGB (Mines and Geosciences Bureau) — landslide and geohazard maps
  • DENR — environmental regulation, reforestation, mining oversight

📌 Quick Check

  • What is a hazard, and how does it become a disaster? (Answer: a hazard is a natural event; it becomes a disaster when it strikes a vulnerable community)
  • What are ipo-ipo, and when are they most common? (Answer: tornadoes/waterspouts, most common during thunderstorms and typhoon season)
  • How does deforestation increase disaster risk? (Answer: loss of roots increases erosion, landslides, and flooding)

days.title: Match Game — Hazard Types
days.content:
🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each hazard, human activity, or agency to its correct description. There are 8 pairs and unlimited retakes to reach 75%.

match.right: A natural event that can cause damage, injury, or loss of life
When a hazard strikes a vulnerable community, causing widespread damage
Small, intense rotating column of air — also called tornado or buhawi
Storm with lightning, thunder, heavy rain — can trigger flash floods
Increases landslide, flood, and erosion risk by removing roots
Reduces flood and landslide risk by restoring vegetation
Monitors typhoons, floods, heat index, and rainfall warnings
Coordinates national disaster response in the Philippines

days.title: Scenario Challenge — Human-Made Risks
days.content:
🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Read each scenario and choose the best reasoning. There are 5 scenarios. You have unlimited retakes to reach 75%.

scenario.text: 🌲 A hillside forest in Rizal is cleared for a new subdivision. A year later, a heavy rain causes a landslide. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A) Deforestation removed the roots that held the soil together, making the slope unstable
B) The rain was unusually strong
C) The subdivision was built on flat ground
D) Nothing — landslides are always random

scenario.text: 🌪️ An ipo-ipo (tornado) is spotted forming over an open field during a thunderstorm. What should nearby residents do?

choices.label: A) Move indoors to a sturdy shelter, away from windows, and monitor PAGASA updates
B) Go outside to take photos
C) Stand under a tree for protection
D) Drive directly toward it

scenario.text: 🌊 A coastal barangay experiences a 5-meter storm surge during a Signal No. 4 typhoon. Why is this surge more dangerous than the wind?

choices.label: A) Storm surges cause most coastal deaths — they flood communities within minutes and sweep people away
B) They are not dangerous
C) They occur only after the typhoon passes
D) They only affect small boats

scenario.text: 🔥 During El Niño, PAGASA reports a heat index of 43°C in your area. What is the main risk?

choices.label: A) Heat stroke and heat exhaustion — especially for outdoor workers and the elderly
B) Flooding
C) Typhoons
D) Earthquakes

scenario.text: 🏘️ A barangay plans to reduce flood risk. Which combination of strategies is BEST?

choices.label: A) Plant trees and mangroves, improve drainage, enforce proper waste disposal, and build with flood-aware design
B) Fill in rivers with concrete
C) Build more houses in flood zones
D) Ignore the problem and wait for the next flood

days.title: Formative Check — Escape the Hazard Lab
days.content:
🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Hazard Lab

You have 3 lives and 6 keys to unlock. You need 75% (5 of 6) to pass. Take your time — read every option carefully.

escape.text: What is the difference between a hazard and a disaster?

choices.label: A) A hazard is a natural event; a disaster is when it strikes a vulnerable community
B) They are the same thing
C) Hazards are man-made; disasters are natural
D) Hazards are always catastrophic
A) A small, intense rotating column of air — a tornado or waterspout
B) A type of typhoon
C) A tropical fish
D) A rain cloud

escape.text: Which human activity MOST increases landslide risk?

choices.label: A) Deforestation on hillsides
B) Planting trees
C) Building on flat land
D) Using solar power

escape.text: What should you do when a heat index reaches 43°C (Danger level)?

choices.label: A) Avoid prolonged outdoor exposure, drink water, and take breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas
B) Exercise intensively outdoors
C) Wear thick clothing
D) Ignore it — the heat index is not accurate

escape.text: Which agency coordinates national disaster response in the Philippines?

choices.label: A) NDRRMC
B) PAGASA
C) PHIVOLCS
D) DepEd

escape.text: What is the BEST way for a community to reduce flood risk?

choices.label: A) Plant trees and mangroves, improve drainage, and enforce proper waste disposal
B) Build more houses in flood zones
C) Ignore the problem
D) Fill rivers with concrete
